parts.instructions: This examination paper contains 100 multiple choice questions only. You must answer all of them. All questions count the same. There is only one best answer for each question; blacken the letter of your choice on the Scantron answer sheet with a pencil. Constants that you may require (printed before Q71): g = 10 m/s², c = 3 × 10⁸ m/s (light in air and free space), speed of sound in air at 32 °F vs = 331 m/s, 1 eV = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J, k = 9 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², h = 6.63 × 10⁻³⁴ J·s, sin 90° = cos 0° = 1.

questions.stem: A pine tree is a member of the kingdom
explanation_steps: A pine is a gymnosperm (a cone-bearing seed plant with 'naked' seeds). The textbook (G9 pp.82–86) puts bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms in kingdom Plantae.
It is multicellular, photosynthetic and has cellulose cell walls – not an animal, fungus, protist or moneran. Answer: C.
tips: Conifers (pine, cypress, juniper) = gymnosperms = kingdom Plantae.

similar_questions.stem: A mushroom belongs to the kingdom
explanation_steps: Mushrooms are heterotrophic, have chitin cell walls and reproduce by spores – kingdom Fungi. Answer: C.

questions.stem: An example of a simple animal is
explanation_steps: Sponges (phylum Porifera) are the simplest animals: multicellular but without true tissues or organs. The textbook's kingdom Animalia runs 'from sponges to vertebrates' (G9 p.62).
A fern is a plant, a mould is a fungus, a virus is not a living cell, and an insect is a complex arthropod. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is an invertebrate?
explanation_steps: Invertebrates lack a backbone. The earthworm (an annelid) is the only one without a vertebral column. Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following is not a viral disease.
explanation_steps: Tuberculosis is caused by a bacterium (Mycobacterium tuberculosis); the textbook lists it among bacterial diseases prevented by vaccination (G9 p.34).
HIV/AIDS, rabies, foot-and-mouth disease and influenza are all caused by viruses (G9 p.42). Answer: D.
tips: Bacterial: TB, cholera, typhoid, tetanus, diphtheria. Viral: HIV, rabies, influenza, measles, polio, foot-and-mouth.

similar_questions.stem: Which disease is caused by a virus?
explanation_steps: Measles is viral; the other four are bacterial diseases. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Option C is printed 'Foot and mouse disease' – a typo for foot-and-mouth disease (a viral disease of cattle). The answer is unaffected.

questions.stem: The physical act of eliminating food that does not get digested is referred to as
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.22): undigested food materials are eventually eliminated; 'this process is called elimination or egestion'.
Ingestion = taking food in; hydrolysis = chemical digestion; assimilation = use of absorbed nutrients by cells. Answer: E.
tips: Ingestion (in) → digestion → absorption → assimilation → egestion (out).

similar_questions.stem: The use of absorbed nutrients by body cells to build new cell parts is called
explanation_steps: Assimilation is the incorporation of absorbed food molecules into the body's cells. Answer: C.

questions.stem: A wave like, rhythmic, sequential motion along the gastro intestinal tract, which propels a bolus or chyme along the tract is
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.34): the bolus is moved along the oesophagus by 'a wave-like muscular contraction or motion called peristalsis', produced by the circular and longitudinal muscles of the gut wall.
Mastication = chewing; emulsification = breaking fat into droplets (bile). Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Bile helps digestion mainly by
explanation_steps: Bile salts break large fat globules into small droplets (emulsification), giving lipase a larger surface. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Once a fluid enters into a lymphatic system, it is called
explanation_steps: Tissue (interstitial) fluid that drains into the lymphatic capillaries is called lymph (G10 pp.85–87).
Plasma is the liquid part of blood; tissue fluid is the name before it enters the lymph vessels. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Lymph is returned to the blood circulation through
explanation_steps: Lymphatic trunks and ducts empty into large veins in the thorax (subclavian veins). Answer: B.

questions.stem: Internal respiration is at the level of the
explanation_steps: Textbook summary (G10 p.111): respiration includes 'the production of energy in cells (internal respiration) and the exchange of respiratory gases between cells and the environment (external respiration)'.
Lungs, alveoli and pharynx belong to external respiration (breathing and gas exchange). Answer: B.
tips: Internal = inside cells (cellular respiration, mitochondria).

similar_questions.stem: Where does the exchange of O₂ and CO₂ between air and blood take place?
explanation_steps: Gas exchange happens across the thin walls of the alveoli and their capillaries (external respiration). Answer: C.

questions.stem: During inhalation, the contraction of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles causes the volume of the chest cavity to

options.E: to be at equilibrium with the pressure.

explanation_steps: When the diaphragm contracts it flattens, and the intercostal muscles lift the ribs up and out, so the chest volume increases (G10 p.112).
Larger volume → lower pressure in the lungs than outside (Boyle's law), so air rushes in. Answer: D.
tips: Inhale: muscles contract, volume ↑, pressure ↓. Exhale: muscles relax, volume ↓, pressure ↑.

similar_questions.stem: During exhalation the diaphragm
explanation_steps: In exhalation the diaphragm relaxes and returns to its dome shape, reducing chest volume and pushing air out. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The organ (s) responsible for detecting changes in the external environment of an animal are
explanation_steps: External receptors (sense organs: skin, nose, tongue, eye, ear) detect stimuli from the external environment (G10 p.142).
Kidneys excrete, lungs exchange gases, the heart and vessels circulate blood. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Receptors that detect stimuli from inside the body, such as blood pressure and muscle tension, are called
explanation_steps: Internal receptors monitor conditions inside the body (G10 p.159). Answer: B.

questions.stem: The fertilization of a human egg by sperm takes place in the
explanation_steps: After ovulation the egg enters the fallopian tube (oviduct); sperm swim up through the uterus and fertilisation normally occurs in the upper part of the fallopian tube (G11 p.39).
The zygote then moves to the uterus, where it implants. Answer: B.
tips: Fertilisation → fallopian tube; implantation → uterus.

similar_questions.stem: In humans, the embryo normally implants in the
explanation_steps: The blastocyst embeds in the thickened endometrium of the uterus. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Any given nucleotide in a nucleic acid contains

options.B: one sugar, two bases and one phosphate.
options.D: one sugar, one base and one phosphate.
options.E: one sugar, four bases and one phosphate.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.2): 'Each nucleotide consists of three sub-units: a five-carbon sugar, a phosphate group and a nitrogenous base.'
So one of each. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
explanation_steps: RNA has uracil in place of thymine (G12 p.5). Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which types of muscles are striated?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.75): 'Both skeletal and cardiac muscles have a striped appearance when viewed under the microscope.' Smooth muscle has no striations.
Answer: B.
tips: Striated: skeletal (voluntary) and cardiac (involuntary). Smooth = unstriped, involuntary.

similar_questions.stem: Which muscle type is involuntary and striated?
explanation_steps: Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle but is involuntary like smooth muscle. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The “backbone” of a nucleic acid molecule consists of an alternating sequence of
explanation_steps: The sugar of one nucleotide bonds to the phosphate of the next, so each strand has a sugar–phosphate backbone with the bases projecting from the sugars (G12 pp.2–5).
Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: In a DNA double helix, the two strands are held together by

options.E: covalent bonds between bases of both strands

explanation_steps: A pairs with T and G with C through hydrogen bonds. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The stage of mitosis, during which the nucleolus disintegrates and chromosomes appear, is known as
explanation_steps: In prophase the chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes, and the nucleolus and nuclear membrane disappear (G12 p.16).
Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator; anaphase: chromatids separate; telophase: nuclei re-form. Interphase is not a stage of mitosis. Answer: D.
tips: Order: Prophase – Metaphase – Anaphase – Telophase (PMAT).

similar_questions.stem: During which stage of mitosis do the sister chromatids move to opposite poles?
explanation_steps: Anaphase: the centromeres split and chromatids are pulled to opposite poles. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The four cells produced in meiosis will have a

options.A: 2n number of chromosomes and differ genetically from each other.
options.B: 2n number of chromosomes and are genetically identical.
options.C: n number of chromosomes and are genetically identical.
options.D: n number of chromosomes and differ genetically from each other.
options.E: 2n number of chromosomes and are genetically identical to their parent.

explanation_steps: Meiosis halves the chromosome number, forming four haploid (n) cells (G12 pp.18–19).
Because of crossing over and independent assortment the four cells are genetically non-identical ('they are genetically non-identical due to the crossing over', G12 p.19). Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: A cell with 46 chromosomes divides by mitosis. Each daughter cell has
explanation_steps: Mitosis keeps the chromosome number: 2n → 2n, so 46. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which blood type will not be possible for children born from a mother with AB blood type and father A blood type?
explanation_steps: Mother AB (IᴬIᴮ) gives either Iᴬ or Iᴮ. Father group A is IᴬIᴬ or Iᴬi and gives Iᴬ or i.
Possible children: IᴬIᴬ/Iᴬi (A), IᴬIᴮ (AB), Iᴮi (B). Group O (ii) needs an i from both parents, but the AB mother has no i allele. Answer: A.
tips: An AB parent can never have a group O child (and an O parent can never have an AB child).

similar_questions.stem: A father is group O and a mother is group AB. Which blood groups are possible for their children?
explanation_steps: Father gives i; mother gives Iᴬ or Iᴮ. Children are Iᴬi (A) or Iᴮi (B). Answer: A.

questions.stem: An example of a genotype is
explanation_steps: Genotype = 'the genetic make up (constitution) of an organism' (G12 p.31), written as the allele pairs it carries, e.g. TtHH.
'A tall pea plant' is a phenotype; R and r are two alleles (not an individual's genotype); haemophilia is a condition (phenotype). Answer: C.
tips: Genotype = letters (TT, Tt, tt); phenotype = what you see (tall, dwarf).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a phenotype?
explanation_steps: 'Round seed' is an observable characteristic (phenotype); the others are genotypes. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: Option B ('R and r') could be read as the genotype Rr by a weak student; it names two alleles, so C is keyed. Option E ('B and C') is therefore wrong.

questions.stem: A tube-like structure that is part of both the human respiratory and digestive systems is the
explanation_steps: The pharynx (throat) is the common passage for air (nose → pharynx → larynx) and food (mouth → pharynx → oesophagus). The textbook describes it under both the digestive system (G10 p.33) and the respiratory system (G10 p.109).
The larynx and trachea are only respiratory; the oesophagus is only digestive. Answer: A.
tips: The epiglottis closes the larynx during swallowing so food goes down the oesophagus, not the trachea.

similar_questions.stem: Which structure prevents food from entering the trachea during swallowing?
explanation_steps: The epiglottis covers the opening of the larynx when we swallow. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a useful contribution of bacteria?
explanation_steps: The textbook's list of useful bacteria (G9 pp.33–35): decomposition, nitrogen fixation, 'secretion of important enzymes' (by gut bacteria of herbivores, which digest cellulose), fermentation, and production of vaccines and antibiotics.
Bacteria secrete their own enzymes, not human enzymes, so B is the statement that is not a (natural) contribution of bacteria. Answer: B.
tips: Compare each option with the textbook headings word by word – the altered word ('human' instead of 'important') marks the distractor.

similar_questions.stem: Bacteria in the gut of cattle are useful because they
explanation_steps: They secrete cellulase, which digests the cellulose of plant cell walls (G9 p.34). Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Genetically engineered bacteria can make human proteins (e.g. insulin), so a teacher might defend E. B is keyed because the textbook lists 'secretion of important enzymes' (bacterial enzymes), not human enzymes.

questions.stem: A child who feeds too little proteins is likely to suffer from
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.8): 'A severe protein inadequacy in the diet results in kwashiorkor', common in children after weaning.
Marasmus = lack of energy (calories and protein overall); scurvy = lack of vitamin C; goitre = lack of iodine. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Bleeding gums and slow healing of wounds are signs of a deficiency of
explanation_steps: These are symptoms of scurvy, caused by vitamin C deficiency. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A biomolecule, that contains glycerol in it, is a
explanation_steps: Fats and oils (triglycerides) are made of one glycerol molecule joined to three fatty acids (G9 p.121; G10 p.10).
Carbohydrates are made of sugars, proteins of amino acids, nucleic acids of nucleotides. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: The building blocks of proteins are
explanation_steps: Proteins are polymers of amino acids. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Arterioles and venules are connected by
explanation_steps: Arteries branch into arterioles, which divide into capillaries; capillaries join to form venules, which join to form veins (G10 pp.60–64).
Answer: B.
tips: Heart → artery → arteriole → capillary → venule → vein → heart.

similar_questions.stem: Exchange of materials between blood and tissues takes place through the walls of
explanation_steps: Capillary walls are one cell thick, allowing diffusion. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is not an abiotic factor of an ecosystem?
explanation_steps: Abiotic (non-living) factors include water, soil, light, temperature, pH and minerals (G12 p.88).
All of A–D are abiotic, so none is 'not abiotic'. Answer: E.
tips: When every option fits the rule, the answer to a 'which is NOT' question is 'None of the above'.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a biotic factor?
explanation_steps: Decomposers are living organisms, so they are biotic. Answer: C.

questions.stem: What type of immunity develops when vaccines are introduced into an animal body?
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.103): 'Active immunity may also be acquired artificially with the use of vaccines … when vaccines are introduced into the body, they activate the body to produce antibodies.'
The body makes its own antibodies (active) after a man-made exposure (artificial). Answer: B.
tips: Active = own antibodies; passive = ready-made antibodies. Natural = infection/mother; artificial = vaccine/serum injection.

similar_questions.stem: A baby receives antibodies from its mother through the placenta. This is
explanation_steps: Ready-made antibodies (passive) acquired naturally from the mother. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The metabolic process called deamination is carried out in the
explanation_steps: Textbook (G10 p.126): 'Excess amino acids not required to nourish body cells are catabolized in the liver by a process called deamination.' The amino group becomes ammonia and then urea.
The kidneys then excrete the urea. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Urea is made in the ____ and removed from the blood by the ____.
explanation_steps: Urea forms in the liver (ornithine cycle after deamination) and is filtered out by the kidneys. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The structural and functional unit of the kidney is the
explanation_steps: Each kidney contains about a million nephrons, the units that filter blood and form urine (G10 pp.128–131; G11 p.85).
Ureters carry urine to the bladder; the urethra carries it out of the body. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Ultrafiltration of blood in the kidney takes place in the
explanation_steps: High pressure in the glomerulus forces fluid into Bowman's capsule. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The endocrine gland that controls the activities of almost all of the other endocrine glands is called
explanation_steps: The pituitary ('master gland') secretes tropic hormones (TSH, ACTH, FSH, LH) that control the thyroid, adrenal cortex and gonads (G11 pp.3–5).
Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which pituitary hormone stimulates the thyroid gland?
explanation_steps: Thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH). Answer: B.

questions.stem: One of the following statements does not describe the function of the skeletal system.
explanation_steps: Functions of the skeleton (G11 pp.52–53): support and shape, protection, movement (with muscles), storage of minerals (calcium, phosphorus) and production of blood cells in the red bone marrow.
All of A–D are functions, so none fails to describe it. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Blood cells are produced in the
explanation_steps: Red bone marrow (e.g. in flat bones and the ends of long bones) makes blood cells. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The organ responsible for controlling the water level and regulation of salt content in the blood is the
explanation_steps: The kidney is the main osmoregulatory organ: it adjusts reabsorption of water (under ADH) and of salts (under aldosterone) (G11 pp.84–90).
Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: When a person is dehydrated, the pituitary releases more ADH. As a result the urine becomes

options.A: more dilute and larger in volume
options.B: more concentrated and smaller in volume

explanation_steps: ADH increases water reabsorption in the collecting ducts, so less, more concentrated urine is produced. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The presence of excess iron in the body leads to a disease called
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.83): 'As deficiency of iron can lead to anemia; … The disease associated with excess iron in the body is called haemochromatosis.'
Anaemia is the result of too little iron. Answer: E.
tips: Too little iron → anaemia; too much iron → haemochromatosis.

similar_questions.stem: A diet lacking iron most likely causes
explanation_steps: Iron is needed for haemoglobin; deficiency causes anaemia. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The neo-Darwinism theory is also known as the
explanation_steps: Textbook (G12 p.65): 'At present, neo-Darwinism is also known as the “synthetic theory of evolution”.' It combines natural selection with genetics.
Natural selection is Darwin's theory; use and disuse is Lamarck's. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: The theory that characteristics acquired during an organism's life are passed to its offspring was proposed by
explanation_steps: Inheritance of acquired characteristics (use and disuse) is Lamarck's theory. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Speciation is the result of the following genetic isolations except
explanation_steps: The textbook (G12 pp.80–81) lists ways genetic isolation occurs: habitat, mechanical (anatomical), behavioural, seasonal isolation, gametic mortality, zygotic mortality and hybrid inviability/sterility – and genetic isolation leads to speciation.
Behavioural, seasonal, mechanical and gametic isolation are all listed, so none is an exception. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Two populations of frogs live in the same pond but one breeds in March and the other in June. This is an example of
explanation_steps: Breeding at different times of year = seasonal (temporal) isolation. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The blood volume in the body is regulated by a hormone called
explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.88): 'Blood pressure: Blood volume is regulated by a hormone called aldosterone. Aldosterone affects the rate of sodium reabsorption, which in turn affects the rate of water reabsorption.'
ADH (= vasopressin, options A and E are the same hormone) is described there for water reabsorption; glycogen is not a hormone. Answer: C.
tips: A and E name the same hormone, so neither can be the single best answer.

similar_questions.stem: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) is also called
explanation_steps: ADH and vasopressin are two names for the same posterior-pituitary hormone. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: ADH/vasopressin also influences blood volume through water reabsorption, so A and E are physiologically defensible; C is keyed because the textbook sentence names aldosterone and A/E are the same hormone (only one could be 'best').

questions.stem: Which one of the following activities is not considered as a mechanism of heat gain in mammals?
explanation_steps: Heat gain (G11 pp.96–97): vasoconstriction of skin arterioles, raising of body hair, shivering, and secretion of adrenaline and thyroxine, which raise metabolic rate.
Sweating cools the body by evaporation – a heat-loss mechanism (G11 p.95). Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which response helps the body LOSE heat?
explanation_steps: Vasodilation brings more blood to the skin surface, so more heat is radiated away. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The water cycle usually consists of different steps. The step that releases water from a plant body is called
explanation_steps: In the water cycle (G12 p.97) plants lose water vapour to the air mainly through their stomata – transpiration.
Evaporation is from water surfaces and soil; condensation forms clouds; precipitation is rain or snow. Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: Water vapour in the air cools and forms clouds. This step of the water cycle is
explanation_steps: Cooling vapour to liquid droplets is condensation. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances has definite shape and definite volume?
explanation_steps: Solids have a definite shape and a definite volume; liquids have a definite volume but take the shape of the container; gases have neither (G9 pp.7–9).
Chalk is the only solid. Tea and beer are liquids; oxygen and water vapour are gases. Answer: E.

similar_questions.stem: Which state of matter has a definite volume but no definite shape?
explanation_steps: A liquid keeps its volume but flows to take the shape of its container. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The nucleus of an atom is
explanation_steps: The nucleus contains protons (+) and neutrons (no charge). Textbook (G9 p.44): 'The nucleus has a positive charge because a proton has a positive charge.'
The electrons (–) are outside the nucleus. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which subatomic particle has no electric charge?
explanation_steps: The neutron is electrically neutral. Answer: C.

questions.stem: The chemical symbol S represents the element
explanation_steps: S = sulphur. Sodium is Na (natrium), silver is Ag (argentum), silicon is Si ('silicone' is a polymer, not an element), and sand (SiO₂) is a compound (G9 pp.80–82).
Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: The symbol of potassium is
explanation_steps: Potassium = K (from Latin kalium). P = phosphorus, Po = polonium, Pt = platinum. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following substances is a compound?
explanation_steps: A compound is a pure substance of two or more elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio (G9 pp.20–23). Water (H₂O) is a compound of hydrogen and oxygen.
Oxygen, carbon and gold are elements; air is a mixture. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a mixture?
explanation_steps: Sea water contains water with many dissolved salts in variable amounts – a mixture. Answer: C.

questions.stem: Which of the following has the same number of electrons as the Argon atom? [At. No.: O = 8, Na = 11, Mg = 12, Al = 13, Ar = 18 and Ca = 20]
explanation_steps: Argon has 18 electrons. Electrons in an ion = atomic number − charge.
Only Ca²⁺ is isoelectronic with Ar. Answer: C. (The others are isoelectronic with neon.)
tips: Positive ion: subtract the charge; negative ion: add it.

similar_questions.stem: Which ion has the same number of electrons as neon (Z = 10)? [Z: Cl = 17, K = 19, F = 9, S = 16]
explanation_steps: F⁻ has 9 + 1 = 10 electrons. Cl⁻ 18, K⁺ 18, S²⁻ 18, Ca²⁺ 18. Answer: C.

questions.stem: All of the following are representative elements, except [At. No: Li = 3, O = 8, Cl = 17, Ca = 20, Fe = 26]
explanation_steps: Representative (main-group) elements are the s- and p-block elements of groups IA–VIIA (G10 p.21).
Li (IA), Ca (IIA), O (VIA) and Cl (VIIA) are representative. Fe (Z = 26, [Ar]3d⁶4s²) is a d-block transition element. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a transition element? [Z: Na = 11, Cu = 29, S = 16, Ne = 10, Mg = 12]
explanation_steps: Cu (Z = 29) fills the 3d sub-level – a transition (d-block) element. Answer: B.

questions.stem: The chemical formula H₂O quantitatively represents all, except
explanation_steps: Quantitatively, a formula stands for one molecule (mass 18 amu) or one mole of molecules (6.02 × 10²³ molecules, 18 g) (G9 pp.83–84, 112–114).
One mole of H₂O contains 1 mol of O atoms and 2 mol of H atoms. It contains no hydrogen molecules at all, so 'a mole of H-molecules' is not represented. Answer: E.
tips: Count atoms from the subscripts: H₂O → 2 H atoms + 1 O atom per molecule.

similar_questions.stem: How many moles of hydrogen atoms are in 1 mol of CH₄?
explanation_steps: Each CH₄ molecule has 4 H atoms, so 1 mol CH₄ contains 4 mol H atoms. Answer: C.

questions.review_flag: The intended exception is E (H₂O contains 2 mol of H atoms, not H₂ molecules). Pedantically 2 mol H = the hydrogen of 1 mol H₂, and C ('18 amu of H₂O molecules') is loosely worded (one molecule has a mass of 18 amu). Teacher to confirm E.

questions.stem: The element that has the highest electronegativity value is
explanation_steps: Electronegativity increases across a period and decreases down a group; fluorine (4.0 on the Pauling scale) is the most electronegative element (G10 p.30).

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following has the lowest electronegativity?
explanation_steps: Electronegativity decreases down group IA; caesium (≈0.7) is among the least electronegative elements. Answer: D.

questions.stem: One of the following is not a physical property of a substance?
explanation_steps: Physical properties (colour, taste, solubility, boiling point) can be observed without changing the substance into a new one (G9 pp.13–15).
'Hydrogen and oxygen form water' describes a chemical reaction – a chemical property. Answer: C.

similar_questions.stem: Which of the following is a chemical property of iron?

options.E: It is attracted by a magnet

explanation_steps: Rusting forms a new substance (iron oxide) – a chemical property. Answer: C.

questions.stem: One of the following substances has the strongest bond.
explanation_steps: The examiner's intention: NaCl is the only ionic compound. Ionic bonding (electrostatic attraction throughout a crystal lattice) is the strongest, which is why ionic compounds have very high melting and boiling points, whereas covalent (molecular) substances melt and boil at much lower temperatures (G10 p.44).
O₂, H₂O, CO₂ and HCl are covalent molecules. Answer: B.

questions.stem: Which of the following is wrong about diffuse reflection?

options.A: Diffuse reflection is caused by irregularities in the reflecting surface.
options.B: Each ray involved in diffuse reflection obeys the law of reflection.
options.C: Diffuse reflection helps us to see opaque objects.
options.D: All the reflected rays involved in diffuse reflection are parallel.
options.E: Diffuse reflection is also called irregular reflection.

explanation_steps: In diffuse (irregular) reflection from a rough surface, each ray obeys the law of reflection, but the normals point in different directions, so the reflected rays scatter in many directions – that is how we see non-luminous objects from any angle (G10 pp.217–220).
Parallel reflected rays happen only in regular (specular) reflection. Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: We can see our image in a still pond but not on a rough wall because

options.B: the pond gives regular reflection, the wall diffuse reflection
options.C: the wall does not obey the law of reflection

explanation_steps: A smooth surface reflects parallel rays as parallel rays (regular reflection), forming an image; a rough surface scatters them. Answer: B.

questions.stem: A 4.0 cm tall object is placed 15 cm in front of a convex lens of focal power 4.0 D. The height of the image, in cm, is
explanation_steps: f = 1/P = 1/4.0 D = 0.25 m = 25 cm (G11 p.33). The object (15 cm) is inside the focal length, so the image is virtual, upright and magnified (magnifying glass).
Magnification m = |di|/do = 37.5/15 = 2.5; image height = 2.5 × 4.0 = 10.0 cm. Answer: C.
tips: A negative image distance means a virtual image on the same side as the object.

questions.stem: When white light enters a glass prism,

options.A: red light is slowed down the most.
options.B: violet light is slowed down the least.
options.C: orange light is slowed down the least.
options.D: violet light is slowed down the most.
options.E: blue light is slowed down the least.

explanation_steps: Glass has a larger refractive index for violet than for red light (n = c/v), so violet travels slowest and is deviated most; red is slowed least and deviated least – this causes dispersion (G11 pp.50–52).
Answer: D.

similar_questions.stem: In the spectrum produced by a prism, which colour is deviated least?
explanation_steps: Red has the smallest refractive index in glass, so it bends least. Answer: E.

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct about a diamagnetic material?

options.A: It is weakly repelled by a magnet.
options.B: It is strongly repelled by a magnet.
options.C: It gets strongly magnetized when placed in an external magnetic field.
options.E: Its atoms possess permanent magnetic dipole moments of their own.

explanation_steps: Textbook (G11 p.73): a magnet 'would weakly repel a diamagnetic' material (e.g. copper, bismuth, water).
Strong magnetisation and hysteresis belong to ferromagnetic materials; permanent atomic dipoles belong to para- and ferromagnetic materials. Answer: A.

similar_questions.stem: Which material is ferromagnetic?
explanation_steps: Iron, nickel and cobalt are ferromagnetic – strongly attracted by magnets. Answer: C.

questions.stem: An emf of 40 mV is induced in a coil of self-inductance 0.2 H. The time rate of change of current in the coil is
explanation_steps: Self-induced emf: ε = L (ΔI/Δt) (magnitude).
ΔI/Δt = ε/L = 0.040 V / 0.2 H = 0.20 A/s. Answer: C.
tips: Convert mV to V first: 40 mV = 0.040 V.

questions.stem: The sharpness of bending of a wave around an obstacle depends on the

options.C: direction of propagation of the wave.

explanation_steps: Diffraction is the bending of waves around obstacles and openings; it is marked when the wavelength is comparable to or larger than the obstacle (G11 pp.171–172: water waves diffract around small boats but not large ones because their wavelength is smaller than the boat).
So the amount (sharpness) of bending depends on the wavelength (relative to the obstacle size). Answer: B.

similar_questions.stem: We can hear a person talking around a corner but cannot see him because

options.B: sound has much longer wavelengths than light and diffracts more

explanation_steps: Sound wavelengths (~1 m) are comparable to doorways, light wavelengths (~500 nm) are not. Answer: B.

questions.review_flag: Frequency (A) is linked to wavelength through v = fλ, but the textbook relates diffraction to wavelength; B keyed.

questions.stem: A small piston of hydraulic lift has a cross sectional area of 4 cm² and its large piston has a cross sectional area of 200 cm². The magnitude of force, in kN, that must be supplied to the small piston to raise a load of 15 kN is
explanation_steps: Pascal's principle: the pressure is the same on both pistons, F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ (G12 pp.51–57).
F₁ = F₂ × A₁/A₂ = 15 kN × 4/200 = 0.3 kN. Answer: D. (750 kN comes from inverting the ratio.)
tips: The small piston needs the SMALL force: multiply by (small area / large area).

questions.stem: A water pipe having an inside diameter of 2.5 cm carries water into the basement of a house at a speed of 0.90 m/s and a pressure of 170 kPa. If the pipe narrows to a diameter of 1.2 cm and rises to the second floor 7.6 m above the input point, the water pressure, in kPa, at the second floor is
explanation_steps: Continuity: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂ → v₂ = v₁(d₁/d₂)² = 0.90 × (2.5/1.2)² = 0.90 × 4.34 = 3.9 m/s.
= 170 000 − 7 200 − 74 500 ≈ 88 300 Pa ≈ 88 kPa (with g = 10 m/s² from the constants table: 170 000 − 7 200 − 76 000 ≈ 86.8 kPa, still nearest to 88). Answer: C.
tips: Narrower pipe → faster flow → lower pressure; higher position → lower pressure.

questions.stem: Which of the following devices works on the principle of photo electric effect?
explanation_steps: The textbook (G12 pp.116–119) lists, as applications of the photoelectric effect: the photocell ('Photocells are of two types: a) Vacuum type photocell and b) gas filled type photocell'), the photovoltaic cell ('a device that works on the principle of the photoelectric effect') and the photomultiplier ('This device works on the principle of the photoelectric effect').
So every option is correct. A (the general photocell) is keyed and B–E are all accepted. The paper probably lost an 'All of the above' option.

similar_questions.stem: In the photoelectric effect, increasing the intensity of light (above the threshold frequency) increases

options.A: the maximum kinetic energy of the electrons
options.B: the number of electrons emitted per second

explanation_steps: More photons per second eject more electrons per second; each electron's maximum KE depends only on frequency. Answer: B.
